articles.title: AI giant Anthropic publicly files for listing on the U.S. stock market
articles.summary: Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) publicly filed its S-1 investor prospectus on Monday , ahead of its planned initial public offering later this fall under the ticker symbol "ANT." The AI lab, helmed by CEO Dario Amodei, has exploded in popularity thanks to its Claude Code AI coding tool and Claude Cowork enterprise offering. As of May, Anthropic was valued at $965 billion, more than rival OpenAI's ( OPAI.PVT ) $852 billion valuation in March. Anthropic's S-1 provides potential investors with their first look at the company's financials , including how much it's spending on capital expenditures related to AI chips and data center leases, as well as how much revenue it's bringing in and what its largest sources are. The AI lab has faced a number of controversies this year, including a run-in with the Trump administration over how the government can use the company's AI models, and current and former employees warning about the potential threat of killer AI. Though experts say those fears are overblown. articles.title: Iran shrugs off Trump's attack threats and says diplomacy is ongoing
articles.summary: What to know about the Iran war today: President Trump said Sunday he was still deciding between reaching an agreement with Iran and taking action to "finish them off." Mr. Trump has kept open the possibility of a new round of major U.S. strikes against Iran . Iranian officials said Sunday that indirect negotiations with the U.S. continue but that Tehran will not change its positions even if Mr. Trump does order a resumption of American attacks on the Islamic Republic.The price of international benchmark Brent crude oil sat around $115 a barrel early Monday after surging last week over supply concerns, as the Middle East and Ukraine crises grind on and the Northern Hemisphere heads into winter, when demand for gas rises. Kuwait sentences 3 to death for alleged plot to kill deputy prime minister, sources say Kuwait condemned three men to death on Monday for plotting the assassination of the deputy prime minister, collaborating with Iran and joining Hezbollah, two judiciary sources told AFP. The three men are all from the Shia Muslim community, which makes up around a third of Kuwait's population. Huseein Abdallah al-Maatouq, a religious dignitary and secretary-general of the National Islamic Alliance, was among the three condemned by the criminal court, the sources said. Another of the trio had been convicted in 2016 of terrorism before being pardoned by the country's emir. He was arrested again in April, the sources said. The men are accused of undermining national interests, collaborating with Iran, planning the assassination of the deputy prime minister and interior minister, and membership of Hezbollah, which is classified as a terrorist group by Kuwait. The court sentenced 11 other people connected to the case to five years of hard labor. Since the start of the Middle East war in February, Gulf countries, including Kuwait, have arrested dozens of people with suspected ties to Iran. Vessel on fire off Iraq coast, U.K. maritime monitor says A vessel was on fire off the coast of Iraq on Monday, according to the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations center, or UKMTO, citing multiple third-party reports. The vessel was situated 63 nautical miles from Al-Faw, a coastal town located along the Gulf between Iran and Kuwait, the maritime monitor said. "Crew status, damage assessment, and environment impact are unknown," wrote UKMTO of the incident, which it deemed "suspicious activity." The agency reminded those transiting the area to do so with caution while authorities investigate what may have occurred. Netanyahu, rivals trade criticisms over Iran amid tight Israeli election race Wrapping up his re-election campaign on Monday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu claimed that Israel could face potential annihilation by Iran if his political rivals prevailed over him. Over the course of a neck-and-neck race, Netanyahu has campaigned heavily on his security credentials, insisting only he can "finish the job" against Tehran and painting his main challenger, ex-army chief Gadi Eisenkot, as soft on Israel's sworn foe. "I think this is a fateful moment for the future of the state, because we have enemies who want to annihilate us," Netanyahu told Israel's Channel 14 the day before Tuesday's vote, adding, "Gadi Eisenkot will not strike Iran." Eisenkot has in turn accused the premier of playing politics with security on the election's eve and citing the Iran threat when it suits him — an allegation that came after a report, citing unnamed sources, said there were concerns within the Israeli army that the war was being politicized. Netanyahu dismissed the report as "rubbish," and Defense Minister Israel Katz said any reports of a gap between the army and political leadership were "entirely baseless and false." CBS/AFP Delegations from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Turkey meet in Iran to try to avert renewed fighting High-level delegations from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey were in Tehran on Monday for meetings with Iranian authorities to try to avert renewed fighting in the Iran war, Iran's Foreign Ministry said. Iran and the three countries party to the Mecca defense pact — Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan — agreed to continue talks after a "first" meeting in Tehran, Iranian state television reported. Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and Ibrahim Kalin, the head of Turkey's intelligence service, met with Iran's top security officials and negotiators to push for a deal between Tehran and Washington. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei told reporters in Tehran that the agenda for the Monday meeting wasn't set, but the talks would "undoubtedly address the most pressing threats to regional security," while Saudi Arabia said in a statement that the delegations hoped to find "ways to de-escalate tensions, enhance regional security and promote its stability." Two regional officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to speak to reporters, told the Associated Press that the war in Yemen and strikes by Iran-backed Houthi rebels against Saudi Arabia were also among the topics discussed during the talks. During the talks on Monday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said that Iran supports any agreement that would deepen regional cooperation, resolve differences and make greater use of the shared resources and capabilities of Islamic countries. The meeting followed Qatari mediators' trip to Tehran on Sunday, which was coordinated alongside the U.S. and came as part of an effort to scale back regional tensions, a regional official, who spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the talks, told AP. AP/AFP Putin to meet Iranian president and Qatari emir on sidelines of Moscow energy summit Russian President Vladimir Putin will hold five bilateral meetings with foreign leaders on the sidelines of the eighth summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF), including with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said Monday, according to Interfax . Pezeshkian said before departing Tehran that his visit to Moscow would include discussions aimed at securing energy transit routes and eliminating insecurity in the Middle East, which he said was caused by the war sparked by the joint U.S.-Israeli assault on Iran almost eight months ago. Saudi-led coalition says three more drones shot down over Riyadh The Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's government in the escalating civil war with the Iran-backed Houthis claimed Monday to have shot down three more drones over the Saudi capital Riyadh, and in the south of the country. In a post on X , coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki announced the "interception and destruction of 3 drones in the Riyadh region and the southern region." He did not specify where the drones came from, but the Houthis have attacked Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones for weeks in retaliation for the kingdom's involvement in the Yemen war. Earlier Monday, al-Maliki said Saudi air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis at Riyadh. The Saudis have struggled to intercept Houthi missiles and drones on the kingdom's infrastructure. Source tells CBS News why report of rift between Netanyahu and his army chief over Iran seems credible Israeli TV station Channel 12 reported Sunday that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had fallen out with army chief Eyal Zamir over an unspecified new directive on Iran. Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz have both denied the reports, but a senior Israeli source with deep knowledge of the people involved has told CBS News the report of a rift seems credible. The biggest tell, the source said, is that the Channel 12 report passed through military censorship. All stories by Israeli media that deal with national security must go through the censor before publication. This is key, according to the source, because it indicates that military brass felt it was necessary for the public to have the information before Israeli parliamentary elections on Tuesday. Had it been false, the military censor would have simply prevented it from being published, the source told CBS News. The other sign the report may be true is that Zamir, according to the source, is not personally opposed to renewed attacks on Iran – he's just opposed to the timing. The source said while there are likely new threats emerging from Iran, the question for commanders is whether new strikes need to happen now. The military appears to believe that nothing requires a response within such a short timeframe, as Israelis prepare to cast their votes, according to the source. Iranian president says insecurity created by the U.S. is harmful to the entire world Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Monday that insecurity created by the United States in the Middle East was harming the entire world, as he prepared to travel to Moscow to attend the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) at the invitation of Russia's president Vladimir Putin. Pezeshkian said the GECF has 12 member countries and, together with its eight observer members, oversees more than 70% of the world's gas supply. He added that a substantial share of the energy needed globally is exported by these nations. "The problems the United States has created by igniting war in the region and bringing insecurity to Europe have disrupted the free flow of energy," Pezeshkian said, apparently referring to the ongoing U.S.-Iran war and Putin's long-standing claim that the U.S. and Europe are responsible for Russia's ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine . He said his visit to Moscow would include discussions aimed at securing energy transit routes and eliminating insecurity. Egyptian parliament gives president authority to send troops to Saudi Arabia Egypt's parliament on Monday approved a request by President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi that allows him to send troops to Saudi Arabia to help defend the kingdom from attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels. Egypt's House of Representatives "approved authorizing President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi to take the necessary measures to support the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia," state-run newspaper Al-Ahram reported. El-Sisi stressed last week that it would only be a defensive mission, "and does not include an attack on Yemen." Under Egypt's Constitution, the president must consult the National Defense Council and obtain approval from two-thirds of parliament before deploying the armed forces on a combat mission abroad. Egypt has managed, so far, to stay out of the recent military conflicts across the Middle East and has been involved in some mediation efforts. Some in the country view that as one of el-Sisi's greatest achievements. But political analyst Samir Ragheb, a retired army brigadier, told CBS News it was time for Egypt to make good on commitments to help secure the region. "This is a time of war, not politics and statements," he said last week. "If Egypt fails to deliver on these promises, they will lose their meaning and amount to nothing more than empty threats." Saudi-led coalition claims to have destroyed Houthi missile tunnels and launchers The Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's government said Monday that its forces carried out a military operation targeting areas controlled by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in response to repeated attacks by the group using ballistic missiles and drones. In a statement posted on X , coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Malki said the operation sought to neutralize "the sources of threat," and included strikes against Houthi military infrastructure. "The operation included the destruction of (5) tunnels used for storing ballistic missiles, (4) ballistic missile launchers, and a missile storage [unit]," Al-Malki said. He added that the operation sought to disrupt supply lines between areas under Houthi control, targeting "fortifications, elements, and military equipment along the front lines inside Yemen." Al-Malki said the operation was conducted in response to repeated Houthi attacks allegedly targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and Yemen. He said the coalition would continue taking "deterrent operational measures" to protect Saudi and Yemeni civilians. He said the operation was conducted "in accordance with the Customary International Humanitarian Law." Earlier, al-Maliki said Saudi air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis at the Saudi capital, Riyadh. Iran's foreign minister praises Iran's resilience Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has praised his nation's resilience after nearly eight months of war with the U.S., crediting civil defense efforts, national mobilization and cooperation between the armed forces and diplomatic service. "The victorious resistance of our beloved country during the enemy's two recent acts of aggression has been made possible only through the solidarity and mobilization of all military and civilian sectors, as well as the proud presence of all segments of the Iranian people on the front lines of resistance," he said in a message marking Iran's Civil Defense Week. Araghchi added that close coordination between the armed forces and the diplomatic service had brought "great achievements" in safeguarding Iran's independence and dignity. He said the foreign ministry would use its diplomatic capabilities to defend the country politically and legally and protect national interests. "It will spare no effort in pursuing this mission," Araghchi said. Last week, intelligence firm Kpler told The Wall Street Journal that the shadow fleet of tankers holding Iran's offshore oil reserves, which it had been selling to China throughout the war against the U.S. and Israel, had run dry. The millions of barrels of crude, held on dozens of oil tankers in Asian water, ran out in mid-October, Kpler told the outlet, with a U.S. naval blockade preventing Iran from replacing the crude being sold to Chinese refineries. The U.S. naval blockade has cost Iran at least $25 billion in oil revenue, according to U.S. Central Command. Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf on Sunday called for a campaign to cut gas consumption by at least 10% , with officials anticipating shortages as winter approaches. Tanker struck Friday in the Strait of Hormuz, maritime monitor says A tanker was struck in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center said Monday. The maritime monitor said it received a "verified time-late report" of the incident, in which "a tanker transiting outbound was struck by an unknown projectile, disabling the vessel." In a post on X , UKMTO said "the crew have been reported safe." Iran claimed to have struck at least four tankers near the strait on Thursday last week, but there was no corroboration of its claims, and President Trump accused the Iranian regime of inventing attacks on commercial vessels in a bid to hike up global oil prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. Israel defense chief denies report of rift between Netanyahu and army chief over Iran Defense Minister Israel Katz on Monday rejected reports of a rift between Israel's army and its civilian leaders - most notably Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu - over the prospect of new strikes in the war with Iran as "entirely baseless." Israel's Channel 12 reported Sunday, citing unnamed sources, that there had been a confrontation between Netanyahu and army chief Eyal Zamir over an unspecified new directive. Netanyahu dismissed the report as "rubbish" during a TV appearance, and Katz characterized it as an effort to cast doubt on the Netanyahu administration's judgement on the eve of close parliamentary elections that could unseat him. "The reports about gaps between the political echelon and the IDF [army] on the Iran issue are entirely baseless and false," Katz said on X , insisting there was "complete" coordination between the two. In its report, Channel 12 said Zamir had demanded a detailed discussion as well as legal guarantees and the signatures of the political leadership before carrying out the directive he had received. The outlet did not offer details of the purported directive, but cited sources saying there were concerns within the army that the war might be exploited for political gain. CBS/AFP Brent crude oil hovers around $115 a barrel after small drop The price of Brent crude oil hovered around $115 a barrel early Monday after surging at the end of last week over global supply concerns linked to the ongoing wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, as the northern hemisphere heads into the gas-hungry winter. President Trump has fueled speculation that he could order a resumption of U.S. strikes on Iran after next Tuesday's midterm elections. The president told Fox News on Sunday: "I have a decision to make: Do I finish it off, which would be very easy to do, or do I make a deal? That's all." Additional U.S. forces, including a third aircraft carrier group, have been sent to the region, though U.S. diplomatic staffing levels have been reduced, and sources told CBS News last week that the overall American military footprint in the Middle East was also being quietly reduced . CBS/AFP Iran says outcome of Israeli elections "makes no difference" Iran's foreign ministry said Monday that the outcome of the Israeli elections in which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is facing a tight race will make "no difference". "It makes no difference to us who, in these elections, takes the helm of a regime that has brought nothing but violence and massacres to our region," said ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei in a weekly press briefing, a day ahead of the Israeli legislative polls. Netanyahu claimed Sunday that Israel had "intelligence signs that our enemies, Iran and its proxies, could challenge us with attacks in order to disrupt the elections." CBS/AFP Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan to hold talks with Iran Monday in Tehran, officials say Senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan will hold talks on regional security with Iranian officials on Monday in Tehran, Iranian and Saudi authorities said. The meeting will follow eight months of war in the Middle East and recent U.S. and Israeli threats of renewed attacks against Iran. "As agreed, Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani army chief General Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin will participate in this meeting," said Ali Bagheri Kani, the deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council. In an interview with state television, Kani said the meeting will also include Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei. Saudi Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Dr. Rayed Krimly confirmed that the kingdom's defense minister was heading a delegation to Tehran on Monday. "The visit comes as part of the continued efforts by the Makkah Joint Defense Agreement countries for de-escalation between parties involved in the ongoing crisis," Krimly said in a post on X. It is aimed at "promoting dialogue and diplomatic solutions, in support of the mediation efforts carried out by the State of Qatar and the Islamic Republic of Pakistan," he added. Conflicting claims after Houthis say they attacked airport in Saudi capital hours after it reopened The Saudi-led military coalition fighting alongside the Yemeni government in the country's civil war said Monday it intercepted a ballistic missile fired by Yemen's Houthis, after the Iran-backed group claimed a new attack on the international airport in Riyadh. A Houthi spokesperson said the group launched attacks the airport on Sunday , just hours after it resumed flights. Deadly strikes by the rebel group earlier this month had forced the airport to shut down operations for more than two weeks . Coalition spokesman Turki Al-Malki said on Monday that air defenses "intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile" fired by the Houthis toward Riyadh and destroyed two ballistic missile launchers in Yemen's capital Sanaa. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said Monday the group "successfully targeted" the airport with a ballistic missile, and struck oil pumping stations with drones. Saree previously warned that Riyadh airport was still "unsafe" and a "military target," as the airport prepared to resume international flights. The airport closure was a major blow for Saudi Arabia, forcing the postponement of the kingdom's flagship investment conference until 2027 and disrupting travel plans for thousands of passengers. Saudi Arabia and the government it backs in Yemen have come under sustained attack in recent weeks from the Houthis as a years-long truce broke down over the summer, shifting the focus of the wider U.S.-Iran war that erupted in February. CBS/AFP Netanyahu warns Iran may use attacks to disrupt Tuesday's Israeli elections Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that Iran and its allies might try to disrupt Tuesday's Israeli elections, warning the Islamic republic against any hostile acts. "The IDF is prepared in both defense and offense," Netanyahu said in a video released by his office on Sunday, using the acronym for the Israeli army. "We have intelligence signs that our enemies, Iran and its proxies, could challenge us with attacks in order to disrupt the elections," he added. "Don't test us. You will suffer disproportionate blows." CBS/AFP Trump says he's weighing deal with Iran against action to "finish them off" President Trump said Sunday morning that he's deciding between reaching an agreement with Tehran and taking action to "finish them off," after suggesting Friday that Washington "may do another little Epic Fury," in reference to the U.S. and Israel's joint military campaign against Iran. "Now, my question is, do I make a deal with them, or do I finish them off?" said Mr. Trump in an interview with Fox News' "Sunday Morning Futures." He also claimed that the U.S. now controls the Strait of Hormuz and criticized former President Barack Obama for the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, or JCPOA, which is better known as the Iran nuclear deal. Obama signed the agreement in 2015, but Mr. Trump pulled out of it during his first term in office. Iran says potential new U.S. strikes wouldn't change its position Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that a potential resumption of war with Israel and the United States would not change his country's positions. The remarks came amid mounting tensions between Tehran and Washington after President Trump said Friday that Washington "may do another little Epic Fury," referring to the U.S.-Israeli campaign on Iran that began on Feb. 28. "Recently, there has been talk of a new war, but I am already thinking about the post-war period. Whether there is war or not, our policies remain the same," said Araghchi during a televised event in Tehran. "They have already done so twice and have seen the results. If they want to try again, they know they will achieve no different outcome from those of the past." Direct negotiations between the U.S. and Iran have appeared to stall for weeks, but Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said earlier Sunday that Tehran had not closed the window of diplomacy and messages were still being passed to the U.S. via intermediaries. articles.title: White House is sued again over media bans as press freedom groups seek wider injunction
articles.summary: Press freedom groups on Monday sued the Trump administration, alleging in federal court that attempting to bar CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House violates the First Amendment rights of ordinary citizens to access information about the U.S. government. The three outlets already won a preliminary injunction halting the government from enforcing the bans while litigation plays out. But the new lawsuit, brought by Columbia University’s Knight First Amendment Institute and Yale Law School’s Media Freedom and Information Access Clinic, alleges that the harms of the bans reach far beyond the three named outlets and deprive American citizens of their constitutional rights to access information. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. “The White House cannot decide what information Americans receive by punishing critical reporting,” said Katie Fallow, deputy litigation director at the Knight First Amendment Institute. “When the White House expels reporters because of their coverage and threatens others with expulsion, it isn’t just the press that suffers - the public loses access to independent reporting and gets something closer to government propaganda.” The lawsuit was filed in federal district court in Manhattan on behalf of six named plaintiffs: Yale law professor Kenneth Roth; Yale history professor Beverly Gage; Lawfare Editor in Chief Benjamin Wittes; journalist Daniel Froomkin; University of Pennsylvania student Ethan Young, editor in chief of the Daily Pennsylvanian newspaper; and New York City high school teacher Peter Schmidt-Nowara. “Media that pedal misinformation and defamation are completely capable of reporting their manufactured stories from directly outside,” a White House spokesperson wrote in a statement to The Washington Post. The Justice Department, which represents the government in litigation, did not respond to a request for comment. Trump on Sept. 18 first said that CNN, MS NOW and Politico would be banned for reporting what he called “fake news.” The three outlets sued and days later won a temporary restraining order from U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump nominee to the bench, that allowed them to reenter the White House grounds. Kelly converted that to a more strenuous and longer-lasting preliminary injunction on Oct. 14, writing that the media companies were likely to succeed in arguing that the bans violated their First Amendment press freedom rights and their Fifth Amendment due process rights. Despite this intervention, CNN has been barred from traveling aboard Air Force One with Trump. Theodore J. Boutrous Jr., a partner at the law firm Gibson Dunn who represents the three outlets, last week threatened to take additional legal action if CNN was not allowed back on Air Force One. The White House has made additional moves to limit press access. It last week prevented Andrew Feinberg, a reporter for the British outlet the Independent, from serving as the designated print pool representative following a fiery exchange with the president. Jacqui Heinrich, a Fox News correspondent serving as the president of the White House Correspondents’ Association, called the decision “retaliation.” “The American public’s right to an independent press depends on reporters being able to do their jobs without fear that challenging the president will cut off their access,” she wrote in a statement. The White House last week also threatened additional restrictions against Politico if it did not retract multiple articles about White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles. The news outlet pushed back on the threats, but did make a substantial correction to one of the articles following the White House complaint. Trump also suggested in a lengthy Sunday post on Truth Social that he is considering moving the press corps out of the White House complex entirely. The plaintiffs in the new lawsuit said that they chose to sue in hopes of winning a broader prohibition against such White House bans - not just a ruling that would allow individual news outlets to regain their press credentials. “As the Supreme Court has emphasized repeatedly, journalists are the public’s ‘eyes and ears’ in spaces they can’t access,” said David A. Schulz, director of Yale Law School’s Media Freedom and Information Access Clinic. “The president’s policy of expelling disfavored journalists harms the public and our democracy.” Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/business/2026/10/26/white-house-is-sued-again-over-media-bans-press-groups-seek-wider-injunction/

articles.title: Microsoft offers voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees as it restructures for AI
articles.summary: Microsoft ( MSFT ) announced on Monday that it was offering voluntary buyouts to roughly 60,000 employees as it looks to reshape its organization for the AI era. "The Voluntary Exit Offer reflects an important part of how we're evolving our approach to change: creating greater flexibility and, where possible, more ways for employees to shape their next chapter," Amy Coleman, Microsoft's executive vice president and chief people officer, wrote in a memo to employees. The company is reportedly offering buyouts to employees in Canada, India, the United Kingdom, and the United States at level 70 and below, which includes some senior-level personnel. The announcement follows Microsoft's first voluntary retirement program , which it announced in May. The retirement packages offered ranged from eight to 39 weeks of base pay, depending on employees' positions and tenure. The offers to staff come as Microsoft plans to spend $190 billion on capital expenditures in 2026, largely tied to its investments in artificial intelligence. All eyes will be on the Big Tech giant on Wednesday, when Microsoft releases its quarterly earnings and provides an update on its capex plans and Azure cloud growth. articles.title: Ramaswamy says the Acton campaign 'defamed my mother' before his attack ad
articles.summary: Republican Vivek Ramaswamy slammed opponent Democrat Amy Acton's campaign on Sunday, saying her campaign “defamed my mother” before he released a controversial attack ad earlier this month. Appearing on Fox News , Ramaswamy was asked whether he regretted releasing an attack ad that featured Acton’s estranged mother , Donna Arthur, calling her daughter a “liar.” “I'll tell you the advice I was raised in: You never start a fight, but if you find yourself in one, you finish it, and you have to stand for what is right and what is true,” he said. “They've attacked me. They've defamed my mother to media silence. It's unbelievable. And yet, at the same time, they'll trot out anything to attack a Republican.” Ramaswamy did not mention a specific instance of alleged defamation. The Hill has reached out to his campaign for clarification and comment. Acton has talked about experiencing physical and sexual abuse, along with neglect, during her childhood. Her mother stayed with her stepfather even after he was charged with sexually abusing Acton when she was 12 years old, according to court documents . Acton’s campaign in August released attacks regarding Axovant, a company Ramaswamy founded that promoted Alzheimer’s medication, and the ad's included his mother. “Today, new reporting details how billionaire Vivek Ramaswamy hired his own mother, who lacked research experience, to manipulate clinical trial data in an alleged ‘pump and dump’ pharmaceutical scheme,” the press release read. Addie Bullock, one of Acton’s communications directors, accused Ramaswamy of “shamelessly profiting off Alzheimer's patients and getting his own mother to manipulate clinical trial data, to make a buck," in a press release at that time. Axovant went public and saw its value shoot up to more than $350 million in its initial public offering before plummeting after the company reported its Alzheimer’s drug failed Phase 3 testing. An investigation by Politifact , a nonpartisan fact-checker, found that Acton’s claims concerning Ramaswamy pushing an “Alzheimer’s drug that he knew didn’t work” and making “hundreds of millions of dollars scamming people” were mostly false. New polling from Fox News showed Acton leading Ramaswamy by 2 points, although her lead is within the poll’s margin of error of 2 percentage points. Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. articles.title: Trump admin's firing of James Comey's prosecutor daughter was unlawful, judge rules
articles.summary: By Luc Cohen NEW YORK, Oct 26 (Reuters) - The Trump administration's abrupt firing of former federal prosecutor Maurene Comey was unlawful, a US judge ruled on Monday, in a victory for ‌the eldest daughter of former FBI director and longtime Donald Trump adversary James Comey. Maurene Comey, who ‌brought criminal cases against Jeffrey Epstein associate Ghislaine Maxwell and music mogul Sean "Diddy" Combs during nearly a decade at the Manhattan ​US Attorney's office, was fired by the Justice Department in July 2025. In a lawsuit against the Trump administration, she alleged that she was fired because of who her father was, in violation of federal laws prohibiting firing civil servants for political reasons and guaranteeing federal employees due process in employment disputes. The case was seen ‌as a test of whether the ⁠Trump administration can swiftly fire line prosecutors like Comey, who are not politically appointed and whose careers tend to span both Republican and Democratic administrations. During his second ⁠term, Trump, a Republican, has sought to expand his authority over federal government entities that have historically enjoyed varying degrees of independence from the White House, including the Justice Department. His critics accuse him of using criminal ​prosecutions ​to punish political foes and reward allies. In court papers, ​the Justice Department argued that prosecutors like Comey ‌are subject to removal without cause by the president or the Attorney General because they are delegated a high degree of executive authority when they represent the federal government in court in criminal cases. Trump fired James Comey during his first term and has attacked the former FBI director for his role in investigating Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election, which Trump won. The Justice Department last year charged James ‌Comey with lying to Congress about authorizing leaks to the ​news media, one of the highest-profile instances of the Trump ​administration using law enforcement to target perceived ​political enemies. He pleaded not guilty and the case was dismissed after a ‌judge found that the US Attorney who secured ​the charges was not lawfully ​appointed. James Comey has since been charged in a separate federal case with threatening Trump. He has pleaded not guilty. In February, Maurene Comey was hired as a partner at law firm Patterson ​Belknap Webb & Tyler. In her lawsuit, ‌she asked Manhattan-based US District Judge Jesse Furman to retroactively reinstate her as a prosecutor through ​December 2025 so she could get back pay and qualify for retirement benefits. (Reporting by ​Luc Cohen in New York; editing by David Gaffen) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/trump-administrations-firing-prosecutor-maurene-151601202.html

articles.title: El-Sayed fires back at Trump with a pointed 'Senator Mohamed' joke
articles.summary: Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D) on Sunday fired back at President Trump's anti-Muslim rhetoric toward him, telling supporters that the president will be referring to him as "Senator Mohamed" if he wins in November. "I get that the president of the United States takes personal offense to my first name," El-Sayed said at a rally in Grand Rapids, Mich. "He doesn’t mind as much when it’s a shared name from the Saudis who are funding his son-in-law’s private equity. Doesn’t seem to mind as much when it’s the Qataris who are giving him a $400 million private jet. He just seems to have trouble pronouncing it when it’s my name." "But y’all, I don’t care how he pronounces my name," he continued. "I don’t even care that he remembers my whole name. Because he can just go on and call me 'senator' after November. I will be Senator Mohamed to you, bro." If elected, El-Sayed would be the first Muslim American to serve in the Senate. Trump has frequently attacked El-Sayed's faith on the campaign trail, mocking his name and alleging the candidate has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist group founded in Egypt that has influenced and supported fundamentalist movements across the region. The president has accused the Detroit-area physician of being a "terrorist sympathizer" and a "jihadist," calling the Michigan Democrat "Mohamed El-Sayed." While rallying in Michigan on Sunday for El-Sayed's opponent, Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), Trump claimed that El-Sayed would "have to go through a metal detector before he's allowed to go into the Senate." Trump then likened El-Sayed to the hijackers behind the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks after introducing speaker David Beamer at the rally. Beamer's son, Todd Beamer, was among the passengers who died on United Flight 93, Reuters reported . "Twenty-five years later, Michigan needs to stand up and fight just like Todd did to stop a jihadist from walking into the Capitol," Trump said. El-Sayed, whose full name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, is Muslim and was born in Michigan to Egyptian immigrant parents. Rogers has also made claims tying El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood, saying at Sunday's rally that the group "celebrated exactly one victory in the United States in the primary this year. Abdul El-Sayed’s." "Meet the Press" host Kristen Welker pressed Rogers on NBC News about Trump's past remarks calling El-Sayed a "violent terrorist" and whether he agreed with the president. "No, I don't," Rogers said. "I've never called him a terrorist. I've never called him a terrorist. This election is about me versus Abdul. I mean, he's a Democrat Socialist of America-aligned candidate who has these pretty radical support groups that don't like America. I think those are issues people ought to decide their election on." Rogers said El-Sayed "just won't answer the question" about any alleged connection with the Muslim Brotherhood and told Welker that his opponent "is getting money from groups that support the Muslim Brotherhood. Money from groups that support Hamas and Hezbollah." El-Sayed has vigorously denied any personal ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, though Republicans have dug up past statements by El-Sayed they say are sympathetic to the Islamist movement that briefly took over Egypt in 2012 and 2013. articles.title: Police arrest 15-year-old boy in Tallahassee mass shooting that left 11 injured
articles.summary: The Tallahassee Police Department arrested a 15-year-old boy in connection with the Oct. 24 mass shooting that left 11 people injured outside Bragg Stadium after Florida A&M University's homecoming football game. Anthony Rivers III was arrested Sunday, Oct. 25 as the alleged shooter in the mass shooting, one of the worst in Tallahassee history, and made his first court appearance the following day. State Attorney Jack Campbell said he will be charged as an adult and transferred from the Juvenile Assessment Center to the Leon County Detention Facility. Rivers, who has faced criminal charges in the past, was arrested on 11 counts of attempted homicide and one count of possession of a firearm by a delinquent, said Alicia Hill, a TPD spokeswoman. The Tallahassee Democrat names minors when they are charged with violent offenses. Exclusive: Teen arrested after Tallahassee mass shooting near FAMU, also linked to mall gunfire "Our investigation indicates that a physical altercation occurred before shots were fired," TPD Police Chief Lawrence Revell said in a hastily arranged Oct. 26 press conference. "At this stage of the investigation, none of the victims appear to have been the intended targets." Detectives believe the incident stemmed from a dispute between people who knew one another. At an earlier press conference hours after the shooting, Revell said detectives believed there was only a single shooter. But police now say additional arrests are possible. During a juvenile court hearing Monday, Oct. 26, Leon Circuit Judge Andrew Sheeran ordered Rivers to be held in "secure detention" while his case is pending, which he said was required by statute given the nature of the charges. When Sheeran told Rivers at the outset of the proceeding that he was in court on 11 counts of attempted homicide, a woman identified by court personnel as his mother said over Zoom, "This is a lie" before she was muted. Assistant State Attorney Linda Berman asked Sheeran to sign an order that Rivers have no contact with the victims or witnesses in the case. "He shall not have access to social media applications such as Instagram, Snapchat and any other applications like that," Berman said. "He shall not have unsupervised access to the internet and he shall be supervised for school purposes only while in the detention center." Sheeran told Rivers he was not to have any direct or indirect contact with the victims, whose initials he read aloud. "Your calls at the detention center are going to be monitored on a speakerphone," the judge said, "and a log will be kept to ensure that you have no contact with any of the victims or witnesses." Sheeran granted a motion that he said was filed by the Police Department to seal the probable cause affidavit, which includes details of the crime and what led to the suspect's arrest. State Attorney Jack Campbell spoke in favor of the motion over Zoom. "This is a continuing criminal investigation," he said. "We would ask that the court keep the probable cause sealed from public disclosure for the sanctity and the security of the investigation and the witnesses involved." 'A night of fear and violence' At least 12 people were injured, including 11 who were shot. Six of the victims were children, including the youngest victim, who is 11, according to TPD Chief Lawrence Revell. A grandmother of one of the victims also was injured. Six remain hospitalized, with one of the victims in critical condition. Half of the victims were male, the other half female. Gunfire erupted shortly before 8 p.m. Oct. 24, at Perry and Manatee streets, an area usually packed with food trucks and vendors during FAMU home football games. It was packed with students, alumni, families and Rattlers fans. “What should have been a weekend of celebration in our community instead became a night of fear and violence for the victims and their families,” Revell said. “While this arrest marks a significant step forward, our work is far from over. We remain committed to holding those responsible accountable and getting answers for every family impacted by this tragedy.” TPD said its officers and investigators worked "around the clock" to identify the alleged shooter. "In the moments immediately following the shooting, our officers rushed toward danger to render aid to victims even before the scene was fully secured," Revell said. "I could not be prouder of the men and women of this department." Police said a "significant influx" of information poured in from the community. Before the arrest, TPD asked the public for any cellphone video or tips from witnesses. "Tips and digital evidence provided by members of the public have been vital to investigative efforts," he said. "But we are not finished." The investigation remains open and active. "This arrest represents progress, but we will not stop working until we fully establish what happened, identify everyone involved and bring the people to justice," he said. "Twelve people were injured Saturday night. Twelve families had to confront something no family should have to face," he continued. "We owe those victims, their families and this community answers." The police "need our community's help. No detail is too small, and no piece of information should go unreported," Revell said earlier. "If you know something, please share it with our detectives. Your information could be the key to holding those responsible accountable." TPD asks community for help To aid in this ongoing investigation, TPD has established a dedicated tip hotline (850-891-4610) and activated an evidence submission website ( tallahasseepd.evidence.com/axon/community-request/public/perrystreetincident) . Police encourage members of the public to securely share photos, videos and other information that may assist detectives. You also can remain anonymous by calling Crime Solvers at 850-574-TIPS with tips and other information. This is a developing news story. Check back with Tallahassee.com later for more. Contact Jeff Burlew at jburlew@tallahassee.com or 850-599-2180. articles.title: Thousands of poll watchers are preparing for an Election Day unlike any other
articles.summary: NEW YORK (AP) — Democrats and outside watchdogs are planning a massive presence at the polls on Election Day driven by concerns that President Donald Trump will further leverage the vast resources of the federal government to interfere with a midterm that could hobble his final two years in office. They won't be the only ones there. A sprawling election protection effort on the left that is expected to deploy tens of thousands of monitors will be met by the largest-ever monitoring program by the Justice Department and still more observers from Republican-aligned groups. The result could be unlike anything seen at the polls in modern times. The effort among Democratic and nonprofit groups includes training volunteers to stand watch outside polling places and report activities they consider concerning. The network includes traditional government watchdogs such as Common Cause and the American Civil Liberties Union plus a flood of volunteers assembled by state Democratic parties, congressional leaders, national activist groups and organizations focused on protecting democracy. The Democratic National Committee's Association of State Democratic Committees created a first-of-its-kind cybersecurity unit staffed by former CIA and FBI officials to monitor and report online misinformation, including artificial intelligence deepfakes , said Jane Kleeb, vice chair of the DNC. That's as Democratic mayors, attorneys general and secretaries of state host tabletop exercises simulating worst-case scenarios, such as a surge of Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials at voting locations or the seizure of ballots and voting equipment . On Capitol Hill, Democratic leaders have assembled a legal team that rivals that of any presidential campaign. “We’ve never done this before,” Kleeb said of the party’s sweeping efforts. But “we’ve never had to deal with the president of the United States saying that he may seize ballots, put ICE agents outside polling locations and other kinds of very clear direct threats to the voting process.” The Department of Justice has already filed lawsuits in California and Alaska that could affect ballot counting or certification . While Trump continues to make baseless allegations of cheating in the election, administration and military officials have said they have no plans to deploy immigration agents or troops to polling sites. White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis blamed “radical Democrats” for creating fears about election security by refusing to enact voter ID requirements and other Republican-backed measures. “President Trump has done more than any other president to ensure we have free and fair elections,” Bis said. Tens of thousands of volunteers trained to observe State Democratic parties have trained an estimated 10,000 volunteers to observe polling places and report anything potentially concerning they might see from federal agents. Common Cause has trained roughly 16,000 more volunteers to stand watch at voting precincts, said Suzanne Almeida, vice president of states for the group. She said a broader Election Protection coalition involving 300 other groups has trained tens of thousands more. Smaller pockets of volunteers from other groups also are preparing to show up, including roughly 100 organized by Senate Democrats and hundreds more from a Democratic-allied group called Save America, which is training clergy members, veterans, teachers and other local community members. National groups such as Indivisible and MoveOn are activating their own expansive networks. There are so many organizations working to protect the voting process — including many that cannot legally coordinate with each other — that some officials involved worry about unintentionally creating chaos outside polling locations. Almeida said Election Day confusion is possible in some precincts but the nature of the threat requires a collective effort. “It will actually take all of us if some of the threats we are most worried about come to pass,” she said. Trump administration sends its own team Harmeet Dhillon, a Trump appointee who leads the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division , was asked on CBS’ “60 Minutes” whether the Republican administration is planning to send ICE agents to polling places. “There is no plan to do that,” she responded. Still, the Justice Department is planning its largest-ever election monitoring effort, with about 1,000 department staff expected to observe voting and ensure federal laws are being followed, spokesperson Kiersten Pels said. That comes after a primary season in which the department said it deployed more than 100 election monitors across hundreds of polling locations. At least one of those placements sparked tensions with local officials. Wyoming Gov. Mark Gordon, a Republican, said the behavior of two monitors during that state's primary was “a bit aggressive” and “irregular.” A Laramie County clerk said the Justice Department monitors arrived at the polls intending to interview voters, but her office didn’t allow it. The department disagrees that the monitors did anything improper, Pels said. She added that the monitors are trained to comply with federal law governing conduct at polling places and won’t “interfere with the voting process.” Democratic lawmakers and voting rights advocates have raised concerns that the Trump administration’s monitors could intimidate voters or abandon the duty they’ve had for decades to protect against civil rights violations. The department plans to send them to every state, focusing on high-population areas, jurisdictions that have had problems in the past and districts with close elections, according to a senior department official who briefed reporters on the condition of anonymity under terms set by the department. The Republican National Committee said its operation involves deploying “election integrity deputy state directors” in 22 states, among them Arizona, Michigan, Georgia and North Carolina. Those workers are the “eyes and the ears of the RNC in the field” who recruit volunteers and organize trainings, said Ally Triolo, the RNC’s election integrity communications director. Their mission is to surface anything that seems unlawful. At the same time, the RNC has enlisted nearly 22,000 poll workers and is recruiting poll-watching volunteers for competitive districts. The poll watchers will “observe the process and help ensure election rules are followed in accordance with the law,” Triolo said. Local election officials prepare for increased attention While federal monitors have quietly observed elections for decades, largely without incident, some election officials are taking precautions. Chris Swope, the city clerk in Lansing, Michigan, said he preemptively contacted law enforcement and his attorney in case federal monitors violate election law, although he expects them to abide by the rules. The Democratic Mayors Association issued guidance to local Democratic officials with detailed instructions about what to do if federal agents appear at polling locations. It notes that federal law prohibits the presence of federal immigration agents, the FBI or other investigative personnel. It also issued a reminder that federal agents are not allowed to be armed at the polls, nor are they allowed to interact with voters or handle ballots or election equipment. Justice Department officials have said their monitors won't be armed and will not interfere with voting. Asked about department monitors being sent to Georgia, Trump told a reporter recently: “They’re not going to do anything other than watch." Some of the poll observations have already begun. Mary Corcoran, Save America's executive director, said her group's volunteers have been monitoring precincts during early voting in Georgia, Michigan, North Carolina and Ohio to help give voters a sense of security. “The fear is the point, and we must do something about it,” she said. “Left unanswered, fear does the work of keeping people home without a single agent setting foot at a polling place.” ___ Associated Press writers Jacqueline GaNun in Lansing, Mich., Mary Clare Jalonick in Washington and Jessica Hill in Las Vegas contributed to this report. articles.title: Republicans face unexpectedly close Senate races in 4 states Trump won easily
articles.summary: Thirty-five Senate seats are up for grabs when Americans head to the polls on Nov. 3. A key handful of them will be critical in determining whether Democrats or Republicans control the chamber next year. Republicans currently control the Senate with 53 seats. Democrats and two independents make up the Senate minority with 47 seats. In order for Democrats to take the chamber back, they’ll have to net four seats in the upcoming election. Republicans can afford to lose up to three and still be considered the Senate majority with the tie-breaking vote of Vice President JD Vance. Some of the races that were closely watched earlier this year have slid from the spotlight as the election grew near. Republicans seem to have abandoned efforts to unseat incumbent Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia and have pulled out of spending in North Carolina, where former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper now seems poised to best former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley to fill retiring GOP Sen. Thom Tillis' seat. As both parties prepare for the final leg of the campaign, here are some of the most closely watched Senate races. Reuters/Getty Images - PHOTO: Democratic candidate for US Senate Abdul El-Sayed in Warren, Michigan, October 3, 2026 and Michigan Republican Senate candidate, former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers, October 9, 2026 in Highland Township, Michigan. Michigan: A bitter fight against a progressive newcomer ABC News rating: Lean Democrat Republican nominee Mike Rogers is no stranger to Senate races -- the former congressmen lost his 2024 bid to now-Sen. Elissa Slotkin by less than 20,000 votes. Rogers is squaring off this time against progressive Abdul El-Sayed, a former health executive who bested a moderate candidate in the Democratic primary. Republicans have gone to great lengths to frame El-Sayed as “radical" over his support for Medicare for all and his positions on immigration. They've also attacked him for his faith and ethnicity. Rogers has falsely linked him to terrorist groups and President Donald Trump has gone as far as calling him a "vicious, violent jihadist" while urging voters to reject him to "preserve our religion, our values, and our heritage." El-Sayed, who was born to Egyptian immigrant parents in Rochester Hills, Michigan, has denied ties to terrorism and called those characterizations Islamophobic. El-Sayed told ABC News Live anchor Linsey Davis last week, "They think they can point to my name and my faith and distract us from the fact that we can't afford our gas and we can't afford our groceries." Rogers told Davis in a separate interview the he thought he was making inroads with traditionally Democratic Jewish and Black voters who are wary of El-Sayed. Michigan has voted for Trump in two of the last three elections, yet Democrats have prevailed in every Senate race since 1994. Reuters/Getty Images - PHOTO: Texas Attorney General and Republican US Senate candidate Ken Paxton  in The Woodlands, Texas, October 9, 2026 and Texas Democratic Senate candidate, State Rep. James Talarico, October 23, 2026 in Austin, Texas. Texas: A primary upset puts Dems in the hunt ABC News rating: Tossup Texans have not been represented by a Democrat in the Senate for 33 years, but Democrats say this could be the year that changes. Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton beat long-time incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in a costly GOP primary runoff thanks to Trump's late endorsement. Paxton, a hardliner and ally of the president, is seen by many Republicans as a harder sell in the general election than Cornyn would have been. Paxton has had several scandals in his time in the public eye. He was impeached in 2023 on allegations of abuse of office, bribery and corruption but was acquitted by the state Senate. He was indicted on securities fraud charges in 2015 but reached a pretrial agreement with prosecutors just weeks before trial in which he agreed to community service, legal ethics courses and pay $300,000 in restitution in return for not having to admit guilt. Democrat James Talarico is a former state representative and Presbyterian seminarian. Republicans have tried to paint the 37-year-old progressive as far-left and radical. Democrats hope Paxton’s lack of favorability coupled with larger concerns about affordability could be enough to end their three-decade Senate drought. Republicans are taking no chances, pouring millions into this race and even opted to hold their inaugural midterm convention in Dallas. The race is the most expensive Senate race in history: Outside groups have contributed more than a quarter-billion dollars to elect Paxton. Over $500 million has been spent on ads in the state, according to AdImpact. Getty Images/AP/Gerald Heikes - PHOTO: Sen. Dan Sullivan, October 6, 2026 in Anchorage, Alaska, Mary Peltola, Aug. 18, 2026, in Anchorage, Alaska, Dan J. Sullivan, June 26, 2026, in Petersburg, Alaska and Gerald Heikes. Alaska: 4 candidates, 2 Dan Sullivans ABC News rating: Tossup Incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan will square off against former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola and another candidate with the same name in another surprisingly close race. Alaska’s ranked-choice voting sends the top four vote-getters in primaries to the general election. Peltola is advantaged by being the only Democrat to advance. In addition to Peltola, Sen. Sullivan faces another opponent on the ballot also named Dan Sullivan, an independent, and Republican Gerald Heikes, who made the final four when the fourth-place finisher dropped out. Republicans, including Trump, have made a point of reminding voters to check that they’re casting their ballot for the “real Dan Sullivan,” and on Oct. 23 he directed the Justice Department to preemptively sue to block certification of the results if the incumbent narrowly loses. Trump won Alaska by 13 points in 2024. AP/Getty Images - PHOTO: Democratic Ohio Senate candidate Sherrod Brown in Akron, Ohio, Thursday, July 16, 2026 and U.S. Sen. Jon Husted, October 15, 2026 in Boardman, Ohio. Ohio: An appointee senator vs. a former one ABC News rating: Tossup The Ohio Senate race features two candidates fighting for their chance to return to the Senate: incumbent Republican John Husted and former Sen. Sherrod Brown, who lost his 2024 reelection bid to Bernie Moreno. Husted was appointed by Ohio GOP Gov. Mike DeWine in 2025 to fill the Senate seat left vacant by Vice President JD Vance. This race will determine who finishes out the remainder of Vance’s term until 2029. This is Husted’s first time on the statewide ballot. Though Ohio has been moving increasingly toward Republicans in recent elections, Husted faces a tough race amid growing concerns about affordability and data centers in his home state. Brown lost his reelection bid against newcomer Moreno by about four points in 2024, though he outperformed Democratic nominee Kamala Harris in the state. The three-term senator is making a pitch to working-class voters concerned about cost-of-living issues. AP/Getty Images - PHOTO: Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Adam Hamilton, Oct. 21, 2026 in Kansas, City and Sen. Roger Marshall, Oct. 21, 2026 in Kansas, City. Kansas: Challenging the GOP's lock on Senate seat ABC News rating: Tossup The Kansas Senate race was not expected to be competitive -- Trump won the state by 16 points in 2024 and Republicans have held both Senate seats in Kansas for nearly a century. Yet even incumbent Republican Sen. Roger Marshall has conceded that it's “quite a close race” this cycle. Marshall, a medical doctor who served in the House before being elected to the Senate in 2020, has largely supported Trump’s policies during his time in Congress. His opponent, Adam Hamilton, has sought to emphasize Marshall’s ties to the unpopular policies that have created economic challenges for voters. Hamilton is reverend of the largest United Methodist congregation in the nation. He has tried to brand himself as an “independent-minded” Democrat but Marshall has said Hamilton is “too woke” to represent the people of Kansas. Getty Images - PHOTO: Sen. Susan Collins in Bangor, Maine, October 15, 2026 and Democratic candidate for US Senate Troy Jackson in Bangor, Maine, October 15, 2026. Maine: Can a 100-day-long campaign unseat an institution? ABC News rating: Tossup Longtime Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins has repeatedly defied the odds, and kept her seat even after being counted out. She’s a moderate Republican who has been more willing than most in her party to break with the president on some issues. But Democrats think Troy Jackson, a former Maine Senate president and majority leader, could put an end to Collins’ nearly-30-year Senate career. Jackson was a late entry into the race after Graham Platner, the original nominee, dropped out following sexual assault allegations. Collins, the chair of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee, has name recognition and a long record of serving Maine on her side and has tried to highlight her willingness to vote against her party. Jackson has tried to show Collins failed to when it counted -- notably, Jackson has accused her of "paving the way" for the Supreme Court to overturn Roe v. Wade by casting the deciding vote for Justice Brett Kavanaugh. Getty Images/AP - PHOTO: Iowa Republican Senate candidate, Rep. Ashley Hinson, October 9, 2026 in West Des Moines, Iowa and Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Josh Turek, Oct. 13, 2026, in Des Moines, Iowa. Iowa: A surprisingly competitive race ABC News rating: Tossup Trump has been rallying in Iowa to support Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson’s bid to replace retiring GOP Sen. Joni Ernst in a race that few thought would be competitive at the beginning of the cycle. There are no Democrats in Iowa's congressional delegation and Trump won the state by a commanding 13 points in 2024. Iowa has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 2008. But rising costs caused by the Iran war have hit Iowa farmers hard. Many see moderate Democratic nominee Josh Turek, a state representative and two-time Paralympics gold medalist in wheelchair basketball, as a formidable candidate against Hinson. articles.title: AI烧钱压力下，微软向6万名员工提供自愿离职补偿，覆盖Xbox、Windows等部门
articles.summary: 微软正在以罕见的大规模的自愿离职计划重塑劳动力结构，此举旨在控制成本，为其大规模的AI投资筹集资金。 据彭博援引微软发言人， 公司将向约6万名员工提供自愿离职补偿，覆盖美国、加拿大、印度和英国，适用对象为副总裁级别及以下人员。 首席人事官Amy Coleman在周一致员工的备忘录中表示，此举旨在为"正在考虑离开公司"的员工提供一条有支持的过渡路径，员工所获待遇与标准离职补偿方案相当。 微软将在周三发布财报，市场关注AI大规模投入是否已开始产生可量化的回报。 截至发稿，微软周二盘中上涨1.1%。 Xbox、Windows等部门全面参与，数据中心等岗位不在其列 据彭博援引知情人士透露， Xbox、Windows、Copilot及财务等部门将全面参与此次计划；但部分员工群体不在适用范围之内，包括专注于数据中心、销售、营销、网络安全及量子计算的相关岗位。 微软发言人表示， 与今年7月面向退休年龄员工推出的自愿离职计划相比 ，公司预计此次接受方案的人数比例将明显偏低。彼时约8750名符合条件的员工中， 逾30% 接受了该方案。 截至今年6月底，微软全球员工总数为22.3万人。自2022年前后公司开始大规模投入AI及数据中心建设以来，员工总数基本维持在这一水平， 这意味着AI支出的持续膨胀已在实质上压缩了其他领域的招聘和预算空间。 科技行业"拥抱AI或离开"的逻辑正在深化 此次离职计划背后是更清晰的人才战略导向。 微软发言人表示，公司希望留用的是真正投身于攻克关键难题的员工 ，这与其他科技公司管理层的公开表态高度一致——持续任职意味着接受更快的工作节奏与变革要求。 这一趋势在行业中并不孤立。埃隆·马斯克2022年收购Twitter后，曾要求员工选择"极度拼命工作"或接受遣散金。据报道，今年早些时候，谷歌一名高管也告知其团队成员，若未能"全力投入"AI，可选择接受自愿离职方案。 谷歌母公司Alphabet去年在多个部门推出了类似计划；Meta Platforms的员工总数则已较2022年末的峰值缩减逾2万人。两家公司均是全球数据中心基础设施的最大投资方之一。 员工如何权衡，公司如何兜底 对于员工而言，是否接受自愿离职补偿通常涉及多重考量：自身储蓄状况、被裁员的潜在风险、当前就业市场的吸纳能力，以及补偿金能否提供足够的缓冲期以实现职业转型。 相较于被动裁员，自愿离职方案通常条件更为优厚，且多适用于薪酬较高的中高级别员工。 微软发言人补充称，若部分顶尖人才选择接受补偿方案，公司也将尝试予以挽留。 Amy Coleman在备忘录中将此次计划定位为各业务部门"调整劳动力结构以适应不断变化需求"的又一工具。 近年来，微软已历经数轮大规模裁员，累计削减数万个岗位。此次以自愿为导向的补偿计划，则代表着该公司在以更温和但同样坚定的方式，推动人力资本向AI时代的全面切换。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: iPad mini首配OLED并支持IP67，国行5499元起售上探中端平板定价
articles.summary: 苹果将旗下最小尺寸平板电脑彻底升级，以屏幕技术换代和防水能力首发为由，将iPad mini的入门价格推至新高，对中端平板市场形成直接压力。 苹果于26日周一发布第八代iPad mini，新机搭载8.5英寸OLED显示屏，并首次获得IP67防尘防水认证，同时搭载A20 Pro芯片。国行128GB起售价定为5499元人民币，美国市场起售价为699美元。与上一代iPad mini发布时499美元的起售价相比，新机价格累计上涨200美元，涨幅达40%。 定价上移直接重塑了iPad mini所在的小尺寸平板价格带。OLED面板的引入与IP67防水设计带来的成本上升，是此次涨价的核心驱动因素。苹果将此次更新定位为"iPad mini有史以来最大幅度的升级"，试图以旗舰级技术规格支撑更高的价格定位。新机将于10月28日开放预订，11月6日正式发售。 OLED与IP67：成本上移的双重驱动 此次iPad mini定价跳升，根源在于两项关键硬件升级同步落地。 屏幕方面，新款iPad mini从LCD切换至OLED，采用Super Retina XDR面板，峰值亮度达1200尼特，是前代机型的两倍以上；对比度提升至2,000,000:1；最低亮度降至1尼特，适应暗光环境使用。屏幕尺寸也从8.3英寸微增至8.5英寸，同时通过将边框收窄24%，维持了整机的紧凑尺寸。 防水方面，苹果通过引入全新"Acoustic Display"声学显示系统，将扬声器整合至屏幕背后，取消了传统开孔设计，从而为整机实现IP67防尘防水等级创造了条件。这是iPad产品线首次达到该防护标准。这一音频架构同时带来了音质升级——专用低音单元通过屏幕传导声音，高音单元则隐藏于玻璃与铝合金机身之间。 机身设计同步优化：新机厚度从6.3毫米降至5.4毫米，Wi-Fi版重量从293克降至255克，整体减薄约14%。 A20 Pro芯片：性能分级策略 芯片配置上，新款iPad mini搭载A20 Pro，该芯片基于台积电2纳米制程，此前已首发于iPhone 18 Pro及苹果首款折叠屏手机iPhone Duo。 苹果在iPad mini上延续了芯片分级策略：128GB与256GB机型配备5核CPU、7核GPU及单颗16核神经网络引擎；512GB机型则升级至6核CPU，并配备双16核神经网络引擎，多线程性能提升最高达60%。 与上一代搭载A17 Pro的iPad mini相比，A20 Pro带来的性能提升幅度显著：CPU多线程性能提升最高60%，图形性能提升最高2.7倍，AI推理性能提升最高4.5倍，统一内存带宽提升超过2倍。 此外，Wi-Fi版本搭载苹果自研N1芯片，支持Wi-Fi 7与蓝牙6；蜂窝版本则首次在iPad上引入C2调制解调器，蜂窝数据速度较前代提升最高50%。新机还新增快充支持，使用35W或更高功率适配器可在30分钟内充至50%。 定价跳升：对中端平板市场的冲击 此次定价调整对iPad mini所在的市场区间影响显著。 上一代iPad mini于2024年发布时起售价为499美元，此后苹果于今年6月将其调整至599美元。新款发布后，起售价进一步升至699美元，意味着在同一年内，iPad mini经历了两次提价。国行5499元的起售价，较上一代发布时的定价存在明显落差，将该产品从此前的中端价格带推向中高端区间。 对比安卓阵营，三星、联想等品牌的同尺寸平板产品在相近价位段提供了更多选择，部分机型已具备OLED屏幕或防水功能，但通常难以同时兼顾两者，且在芯片性能与生态整合层面与苹果存在差距。苹果此次以OLED、IP67与A20 Pro的组合定价699美元，实质上是在主动拉高这一品类的价值锚点。 值得注意的是，新机仍未引入ProMotion高刷新率技术，屏幕刷新率维持在60Hz，这在同价位竞品中已属相对保守，或将成为部分潜在买家的顾虑。 苹果OLED普及战略与供应链影响 iPad mini此次换用OLED，是苹果在平板产品线系统性推进OLED技术的重要节点。此前，OLED已率先应用于iPad Pro系列，iPad mini的跟进意味着该技术正从旗舰向更广泛的产品线延伸。 从供应链角度看，iPad mini体量虽不及iPhone，但其OLED需求的增加将进一步扩大苹果对面板供应商的采购规模，有助于摊薄单位成本，并为后续在iPad Air等产品线推广OLED积累量产经验。 知名苹果分析人士Mark Gurman指出，新款iPad mini是苹果本周密集发布新品的开端。苹果计划本周晚些时候推出搭载M6芯片的新款iMac和14英寸MacBook Pro，并将在本周末发布首款触摸屏MacBook Pro。苹果还将于周三在洛杉矶举行发布活动，供媒体和内容创作者体验上述新设备。 iPad mini的OLED化，标志着苹果在平板产品线的技术升级路径愈发清晰：以屏幕技术换代为核心驱动力，逐步上移各产品线的价格定位，同时借助自研芯片与生态优势，在竞争日趋激烈的平板市场维持溢价空间。 风险提示及免责条款 articles.title: 和黄医药赛沃替尼全球Ⅲ期研究告捷，肺癌耐药患者中位生存期延长近5个月
articles.summary: 10月26日，和黄医药公布赛沃替尼全球Ⅲ期临床研究结果。与传统铂类双药化疗相比，其自主研发的赛沃替尼与阿斯利康已上市的第三代EGFR靶向药奥希替尼联合使用，将特定肺癌耐药患者的死亡风险相对降低32%，中位总生存期从12.9个月延长至17.8个月，增加近5个月。 这项研究结果已于10月25日在西班牙马德里举行的2026年欧洲肿瘤内科学会（ESMO）年会主席论坛上公布，并同步发表于《新英格兰医学杂志》。 不过，这一治疗效果并不适用于所有肺癌患者。研究针对的是携带EGFR基因突变、在奥希替尼治疗后病情进展，同时伴有高水平MET过表达或扩增的局部晚期或转移性非小细胞肺癌患者。 除了针对耐药患者的研究，和黄医药同期公布的另一项中国Ⅲ期临床研究，还将赛沃替尼与奥希替尼的联合治疗推进至初始治疗阶段，为其后续拓展适应症及全球商业化提供了新的临床依据。 耐药治疗取得生存获益 肺癌靶向药耐药一直是晚期肺癌治疗面临的难题。 EGFR（表皮生长因子受体）和MET（间质上皮转化因子受体）都是与肿瘤生长有关的蛋白靶点。奥希替尼通过抑制EGFR信号通路发挥作用，但部分患者在用药一段时间后，癌细胞会通过MET信号通路继续生长，从而对原有治疗产生耐药。 赛沃替尼是一款针对MET靶点的口服抑制剂。将其与奥希替尼联合使用，目的在于同时抑制EGFR和MET两条信号通路，从而克服部分患者的耐药问题。 为验证这一治疗思路，研究者开展了代号为SAFFRON的全球Ⅲ期临床研究。该研究采用随机、开放标签、多中心设计，覆盖29个国家的230个研究中心，共纳入338名奥希替尼治疗后病情进展、伴MET异常的局部晚期或转移性非小细胞肺癌患者。 其中，联合治疗组同时口服赛沃替尼和奥希替尼两种靶向药，对照组则接受铂类药物联合培美曲塞的传统化疗。 研究主要评价无进展生存期（PFS），即患者从研究规定的起点到疾病进展或死亡的时间；关键次要评价指标为总生存期（OS），即从研究规定的起点到患者死亡的时间。 数据显示，联合治疗组的中位OS为17.8个月，化疗组为12.9个月，延长4.9个月，死亡风险相对降低32%。治疗一年时，两组患者的生存率分别为70%和53%。 PFS方面，联合治疗组为7.6个月，化疗组为5.4个月，疾病进展或死亡风险相对降低45%。一年无进展生存率分别为36%和10%。 安全性方面，联合治疗组和化疗组发生3级及以上、所有原因导致的治疗期间不良事件的比例分别为64%和63%，未发现新的安全性信号。不过，联合治疗组发生严重不良事件的比例为41%，高于化疗组的28%，仍需关注联合用药的安全性。 两种靶向药均可口服，能够减少静脉化疗带来的输液负担，但患者仍需定期复查并接受不良反应监测。 SAFFRON全球主要研究者、上海交通大学医学院附属胸科医院上海市肺部肿瘤临床医学中心主任陆舜表示，这些结果有望为约三分之一在奥希替尼治疗后出现MET驱动耐药的EGFR突变非小细胞肺癌患者确立新的全球治疗标准。 他同时强调，研究结果凸显了通过MET检测指导患者后续治疗的必要性。 联合疗法向一线治疗延伸 相比于耐药后的治疗，赛沃替尼的另一项Ⅲ期研究SANOVO，尝试将联合用药提前至初始治疗阶段。 SANOVO是一项在中国开展的随机、双盲、多中心Ⅲ期临床研究，针对此前尚未接受系统治疗、携带EGFR突变且伴MET过表达的局部晚期或转移性非小细胞肺癌患者。 与SAFFRON不同，这项研究的对照组并非传统化疗，而是单独使用奥希替尼，以检验从初始治疗阶段增加赛沃替尼，能否进一步改善患者预后。 结果显示，赛沃替尼联合奥希替尼组的中位PFS达到24.9个月，奥希替尼单药组为13.8个月，延长11.1个月，疾病进展或死亡风险相对降低44%。 在MET高表达患者中，联合治疗组的中位PFS为24.8个月，单药组为11.1个月，延长13.7个月。 OS方面，联合治疗组为44.5个月，对照组为34.9个月，相差9.6个月；三年生存率分别为67.4%和47.4%。 不过，和黄医药目前将SANOVO研究的OS结果描述为具有临床意义的改善，尚未明确披露其是否达到预设的统计学显著性标准。这与SAFFRON已证实具有统计学显著性的OS获益仍有区别。 两项研究共同指向赛沃替尼治疗定位的变化。 此前，赛沃替尼与奥希替尼的联合用药主要面向EGFR靶向药治疗后出现耐药的特定患者。而SANOVO尝试将其向一线治疗延伸，通过初始阶段的MET检测，筛选出可能从双靶向治疗中获益的患者。 这不仅意味着治疗时机提前，也可能扩大赛沃替尼的适用人群。从耐药后的部分患者，进一步覆盖初始治疗阶段伴MET过表达的人群，有望为赛沃替尼拓展新的市场空间。 但这一空间能否兑现，仍取决于后续适应症审批、临床应用及市场竞争情况。 全球商业化进入关键阶段 赛沃替尼由和黄医药自主发现和研发，并与阿斯利康共同开发，全球商业化由阿斯利康负责。 双方早在2011年便达成赛沃替尼的全球许可、共同开发及商业化合作协议。按照相关安排，阿斯利康负责中国以外地区的主要临床开发及商业化工作，和黄医药则可通过里程碑付款及销售分成分享产品收益。 根据和黄医药年报，赛沃替尼若在中国以外市场实现商业化，公司有权获得相关销售额9%至13%的分级特许权使用费，并根据约定取得相应的里程碑付款。 这也意味着，赛沃替尼的海外上市进展，不仅关系到药物的国际市场覆盖，还将影响和黄医药未来的授权合作收益。 目前，赛沃替尼与奥希替尼联合方案已于2025年6月在中国获批，用于EGFR靶向药治疗后病情进展、伴MET扩增的部分局部晚期或转移性非鳞状非小细胞肺癌患者。 但已获批的患者范围与SAFFRON研究并不完全相同。前者要求MET扩增，而SAFFRON还纳入了符合标准的MET高水平过表达患者。 海外方面，针对耐药患者的联合疗法上市申请已经提交美国食品药品监督管理局（FDA），欧洲和日本的申报工作也在推进。 在一线治疗方面，和黄医药计划基于SANOVO研究结果，于2026年底在中国提交新的适应症上市申请。 此前，和黄医药另一款自主研发的抗癌药呋喹替尼，已经先后在美国、欧盟和日本获批上市，并由武田制药负责中国以外市场的商业化。 如果赛沃替尼后续顺利获得美国、欧盟和日本市场批准，将成为和黄医药继呋喹替尼之后，又一款进入全球主要医药市场的原创新药。 不过，临床研究成功并不意味着商业价值已经兑现。 赛沃替尼仍需跨过海外监管审评、市场准入和商业推广等环节，其未来销售规模还将受到目标患者数量、MET检测普及程度、其他耐药治疗方案竞争以及药品定价等因素的影响。 对于和黄医药而言，这两项Ⅲ期研究的意义，是为赛沃替尼提供了进一步进入全球市场、并从耐药治疗向一线治疗拓展的临床依据。接下来，如何将研究中的生存获益转化为实际获批适应症和商业收入，将成为检验其全球化价值的关键。 风险提示及免责条款 articles.title: 中信证券发布三季报：前三季利润增32.66%，单季波动不掩年内向好
articles.summary: “券商一哥”中信证券日前发布三季报“成绩单”。 该公司三季报显示，截至2026年9月末，中信证券总资产已跃升至2.35万亿元，较上年末增长12.88%。公司前三季度实现归母净利润突破300亿元大关，达到310.22亿元，同比增速32.66%。公司的加权平均净资产收益率重回两位数达到10.21%。 不过，如果考虑单季度业绩，中信证券的营收和利润都出现波动，今年三季度同比表现明显弱于去年同期。当然，这并没有影响其作为行业领头羊的地位。相反在波动中，中信证券整体的抗风险能力，更加明显。 前三季营收利润双增 从年内整体表现来看，中信证券2026年1-9月实现营业收入665.90亿元，同比增长18.60%；实现归属于上市公司股东的净利润310.22亿元，同比大幅增长32.66%；扣非净利润更是达到312.32亿元，同比大增34.47%，基本每股收益达2.01元/股，盈利能力延续前期持续增长态势。 但从单季度表现来看，今年第三季度受市场环境、基数效应以及金融工具处置节奏的影响，中信证券的单季业绩出现一定波动。单季实现营业收入168.98亿元，同比下降26.59%；单季归母净利润76.79亿元，同比下降20.19%。 不过，尽管单季数据有所回落，但拉长周期看，中信证券前三季度经营活动产生的现金流量净额高达1267.79亿元，同比暴增125.58%，显示出公司主营业务造血能力，以及航母级的资产和业务规模，造就了很充裕的流动性。 轻资本业务高歌猛进 透过利润表可以清晰地看到，中信证券前三季度手续费及佣金净收入高达326.31亿元（同比增长32.86%），核心业务板块呈现出“多点开花”的态势： 财富管理（经纪业务）方面： 前三季度，中信证券的经纪业务手续费净收入达到147.30亿元，较上年同期的109.39亿元大幅增长。这表明在市场交投活跃度变化的背景下，公司凭借庞大的客户基础和持续的财富管理转型，保持了较强的变现能力。 投资银行业务方面： 在行业投行收入普遍承压的当下，中信证券投行业务手续费净收入达到51.24亿元，较上年同期的36.89亿元实现强势增长。在IPO、再融资及并购重组领域，中信依然处于绝对龙头地位，头部集中效应愈发明显。 资产管理业务方面： 前三季度贡献手续费净收入108.67亿元，较上年同期的87.03亿元稳步提升。值得一提的是，截至2026年9月末，华夏基金的母公司管理资产规模高达2.86万亿元，第三季度单季即实现净利润5.81亿元，为中信证券的大资管版图提供了源源不断的利润增量。 自营与衍生品业务方面： 呈现出显著的结构性调整态势。虽然前三季度公司“投资收益”为179.78亿元（同比下降45.25%，主要系处置金融工具投资收益减少），但“公允价值变动收益”迎来了惊人的大爆发，录得131.29亿元（上年同期为亏损4.24亿元），财报指明这主要归功于衍生金融工具公允价值的变动。两者结合来看，整体自营与交易盘面依然保持了超310亿元的高水平收入。 此外，得益于货币资金及结算备付金、融资融券利息收入增加，公司前三季度利息净收入达32.23亿元，同比暴增319.68%。 大股东期内真金白银“力挺” 除了亮眼的营收和利润指标，中信证券这份三季报中还隐藏着几个的“潜在亮点”： 其一，财报显示，公司前三季度信用减值损失为-4.37亿元（即减值准备转回），而上年同期为计提损失6.48亿元。这一数据的逆转，主要源于买入返售金融资产及融出资金减值准备的转回，说明公司前期对风险的评估出清较为彻底。 其二，大股东“真金白银”拿钱力挺，三季度内中信H股定增顺利落地。公司第一大股东中信金控以现金全额认购8.03亿股（发行价23.13港元/股），持股比例从19.84%大幅跃升至23.96%。 其三，拿到定增资金后，中信证券完成了对全资子公司中信证券国际首批100亿元人民币等值港元的增资，持续加码国际化业务；另一方面，对中信期货完成首批20亿元增资（注册资本增至96亿元）。这两项举措精准指向了跨境业务和场内外衍生品市场，战术和战略意义都很明显。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: AI泡沫承压：这是大甩卖的终点，还是下一个买入时机？
articles.summary: 科技板块正承受多重压力，对冲基金大举削减敞口，波动率警示信号频闪，与此同时，AI融资成本攀升、信用风险交织蔓延，令这轮AI热潮面临日益严峻的资金考验。 过去两周，据高盛数据， 全球科技股遭到约200亿美元的净卖出，抛售强度已触及-3.3个标准差的极端水平。 纳斯达克100指数（NDX）目前仍困于自5月以来的震荡区间，29000点的期货关口与其下方约28500点的200日均线，构成当前最关键的技术支撑带。 摩根大通方面，其分析师Privorotsky指出，尽管AI需求依然强劲，但融资环境正在收紧—— 年内AI基础设施债务融资规模已逾5000亿美元，超大规模云服务商的融资成本较此前上升约120个基点。 英伟达与其GPU客户之间的融资关联，正被视为潜在的信用风险传导链条，一旦GPU运营商资金链趋紧，压力或将反馈至上游供应商。 仓位清洗：与7月惊人相似 本轮科技股抛售的规模与烈度，令市场联想起今年7月的那次回调。 高盛数据显示，过去两周TMT板块累计卖出约200亿美元，已接近7月抛售期间的230亿美元。受冲击最重的交易品种，价格走势几乎如出一辙。 不同之处在于，标普500指数本轮仅下跌约2.4%，低于7月3.4%的跌幅，指数层面的波动相对收敛。 与此同时，高盛风险偏好指标录得有记录以来最大单次跌幅之一，跌至2025年4月以来的最低水平。TMT板块基本面净敞口降至年内低点，尽管总敞口仍处于第63百分位——这意味着净仓位虽已压缩，但总杠杆仍是当前潜在痛点所在。 科技恐慌溢价：高达98百分位 恐慌情绪并未均匀分布于整个市场，而是高度集中在科技板块。 高盛分析显示，NDX与SPX之间的波动率利差已急速扩张至五年区间的第98百分位，上周四单日扩张幅度更创五年来第二大纪录。科技板块专属的波动率定价相对于大盘整体波动已处于异常昂贵的水平，由此催生出潜在的相对价值交易机会。AI相关股票之间的联动性显著增强，但指数层面的波动率整体仍保持相对克制。 AI融资测试：超大规模云厂商成关键变量 本周，谷歌、微软、亚马逊的财报密集披露，市场关注的焦点已超越资本开支指引本身。 据摩根大通，年内AI基础设施债务吸收规模已超5000亿美元，超大规模云服务商融资成本上升约120个基点。在此背景下，市场真正在意的问题是： 积压订单能否有效转化为营收，以及下一轮投资扩张将如何取得融资。 值得注意的是，AI相关信用违约互换（CDS）利差近期明显走阔，但摩根大通认为，这在很大程度上并非反映基本面恶化，而是银行机构为对冲自身持续扩张的数据中心敞口而主动买入保护的结果。CDS与现金债券之间的利差扩大，或正在形成新的相对价值机会。 英伟达生态系统的信用传导风险 英伟达与其GPU客户之间的融资关系，正被摩根大通识别为AI信用压力潜在的传导路径。 以CoreWeave为代表的GPU运营商，依赖客户融资与信用支持维持AI基础设施的扩张。这一模式在支撑增长的同时，也制造了高度相关的下行风险：一旦GPU运营商遭遇融资紧缩，压力将沿供应链向上传导，最终反馈至英伟达等上游供应商。费城半导体指数（SOX）目前正测试200日均线支撑，为这一风险路径增添了重要的技术层面参照。 美国投资，亚洲受益——也最先受损 AI资本开支热潮在拉动美国国内需求的同时，大量资金正流向海外，形成不对称的外溢效应。 据TS Lombard数据，科技出口占GDP比重，韩国接近20%。这意味着，若AI资本开支出现大幅收缩，亚洲出口经济体将首当其冲，承受不成比例的冲击；而美国国内经济实际获得的提振，可能远小于表面的投资规模所暗示的水平。 AI崩溃悖论：利率敏感板块或意外受益 TS Lombard经济学家Dario Perkins提出了一个反直觉的逻辑：AI投资热潮的终结，未必是全面的经济灾难。 他认为，当前AI资本开支的急速扩张正在助推通胀，并使利率维持在更高水平，对房地产等利率敏感板块形成持续挤压。若AI资本开支大幅回落，美联储将获得空间更为积极地降息，从而重新激活非科技领域的需求，并对整体经济下行形成缓冲。换言之，下一轮AI热潮终结后的受益者，恰恰可能是此前在这波浪潮中被边缘化的板块。 潜在买入窗口：条件尚未完全成熟 摩根大通对科技板块基本面维持建设性判断，但同时提示半导体定价可持续性不足及新兴云计算（neocloud）融资压力等风险，软件板块相对韧性较强。 该行认为，11月初或将出现潜在的买入窗口，但条件尚未完全兑现：仓位须进一步充分出清，超大规模云厂商必须确认资本开支方向，半导体盈利需要经受住考验，信用利差亦需回归收窄。上述条件缺一，反弹的可持续性便存疑。对于投资者而言，当前市场既非一目了然的清仓信号，亦非无条件的抄底时机——答案，或许就藏在本周几家科技巨头的财报之中。 风险提示及免责条款
